name: Autodesk Maya
tagline: Autodesk's industry-standard 3D suite for modeling, rigging, animation, simulation and rendering.

pricing.basis: per seat, monthly or annual subscription
pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified. Autodesk sells Maya as a per-seat subscription in the expensive-professional-tool bracket, but no figure is asserted here.

verdictSummary: Maya is not an app, it is roughly thirty years of accreted computational geometry, deformation math, solvers and a renderer, wrapped in a UI that whole film and games industries have muscle memory for. An agent can absolutely build you a 3D viewer, a keyframe timeline, even a basic skinned-mesh playback tool in a session. What it cannot do in one shot is NURBS and subdivision modeling, a production rigging system, nCloth and Bifrost simulation, UV tooling, Arnold-quality rendering, USD and FBX interchange that studios actually trust, and the MEL/Python plugin ecosystem your pipeline is built on. The honest consolation is a small local animation toy, not a replacement. If you genuinely only need to pose and keyframe existing models, Blender is free and already won that argument.
coreLoopDIY: Loads a glTF model in the browser, lets you keyframe object and bone transforms on a scrubbable timeline, and exports the result back out as animated glTF.
requirements: Node 20+ and a modern browser with WebGL2
glTF or FBX models you already own, since there is no modeling toolset here
A GPU that can handle real-time preview of your scene
whatYouLose: All actual modeling: polygon, NURBS, subdivision, sculpting, booleans, retopology
Rigging and deformation: skinning tools, IK/FK, constraints, blend shapes, muscle and skin solvers
Simulation: cloth, hair, fluids, particles, Bifrost, plus anything resembling stable solver behavior
Production rendering: Arnold, shading networks, AOVs, render layers, and a renderer anyone will accept a frame from
Pipeline reality: USD and FBX round-trips, MEL/Python plugins, studio asset management, and artists who already know the hotkeys
moatNotes: The switching cost is not file format lock-in, it is tens of thousands of trained hands and every studio pipeline script written since the 1990s.
whyPeopleStillPay: Studios pay because Maya is where the labor market is. A rigger you hire next month already knows it, your pipeline tools already target it, and your clients expect scenes they can open. On top of that, the software itself is thousands of person-years of solver and deformer work that nobody is reproducing over a weekend, and the price is rounding error against a single animator's salary. Individuals mostly should not pay at all: Blender covers the same surface for free and is better supported for solo work.
notes: A keyframe timeline is a weekend; a modeling, rigging and simulation suite is not. The moat is thirty years of solver and deformer engineering plus every studio pipeline and trained artist already built around it.
prompt:
Build a local, offline 3D keyframe animation tool. This is a deliberately small consolation for Maya, not a clone: no modeling, no simulation, no renderer.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Vite + TypeScript, no framework, plain DOM for UI
- three.js for the viewport, GLTFLoader for import, GLTFExporter for export
- Zustand for state, or a single plain store module if you prefer
- No backend, no accounts, no telemetry, no network calls at runtime

In scope:
1. Viewport: perspective camera with orbit/pan/zoom, grid, one directional light plus ambient, optional environment from a local HDR file if the user drops one in /public.
2. Import: drag and drop a .glb or .gltf file. Show a scene outliner tree of nodes, including bones.
3. Selection: click a node in the outliner or in the viewport to select it. Show transform gizmos (translate, rotate, scale) via TransformControls, with keyboard shortcuts W/E/R.
4. Timeline: fixed 24 or 30 fps, user-settable length in frames, scrubber, play/pause/loop. Keyframe the selected node's position, rotation and scale with a Set Key button and the S shortcut.
5. Keys render as dots on a per-node track row. Allow dragging a key to another frame and deleting it with Delete.
6. Interpolation: linear and step per track, selectable. No graph editor.
7. Playback samples the keyframes and writes transforms each frame; playback must be smooth on a 100k-triangle model.
8. Export: bake tracks into a THREE.AnimationClip and export the scene as .glb with GLTFExporter. Also offer save/load of the raw project as a .json file.
9. Persist the current project to IndexedDB on change so a reload does not lose work.

Explicitly out of scope, do not attempt: mesh editing, UVs, skin weight painting, IK, constraints, physics, cloth, materials editing beyond showing what imported, ray tracing, video export.

Ship a README stating clearly what this cannot do. Secrets: none needed, so do not add a .env. Keep it under about 2000 lines and make it run with npm install && npm run dev.
